summary: Specifies the protocol that implements Realm Specific IP. It lets an RSIP host negotiate with a gateway and lease some of the gateway's addressing parameters so the host can reach the global network. It runs at the application layer using its own port. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RSIP lets a host request public addressing resources from a gateway instead of having the gateway translate each packet's addresses. The host uses the assigned resources and tunnels packets to the gateway for forwarding.

questions: how does a host lease addresses from an rsip gateway
how is rsip different from nat
subtitle: A host-gateway protocol for leasing public addressing resources and carrying packets through a private realm.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translation changes packet addresses and sometimes ports. The RFC notes that this can interfere with protocols that carry addresses in their payload or require addresses to remain unchanged.
tldr.mechanism: RSIP lets a host register with a gateway and lease an address or address-and-port resources. The host tunnels packets to the gateway, which uses its bindings to forward traffic between the host and public network.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3103 is Experimental. The IESG note says complete implementation requires significant host and gateway changes and advises weighing the costs and benefits against other approaches to address shortage.

facts.label: UDP retry recommendation
facts.value: 12.5 ms initial; up to six retries

today: RFC 3103 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. The IESG note calls out host and gateway changes, possible interoperability problems and operational complexity.

sections.title: Why the RFC Defines RSIP
sections.content:
A Network Address Translator (NAT) changes addresses on packets crossing between routing realms, and may also change transport ports. The RFC notes that protocols carrying addresses or ports in their payload may need an application-layer gateway, while protocols that require unchanged addresses may not work through a NAT.

Realm Specific IP (RSIP) uses a different arrangement. A gateway assigns public parameters to a host, which uses those values in packets. This requires changes to hosts, but does not require an application-layer gateway in the RSIP gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT changes packet addresses as they cross a network boundary. RSIP instead assigns public addressing resources to a host, which then uses them in its own packets.

sections.title: Hosts, Gateways and Tunnels
sections.content:
An RSIP host runs a client, and an RSIP gateway runs a server. The gateway owns public addresses and manages resources assigned to hosts. When it grants a binding, it records the association between the host's local addressing and the assigned public resources.

The host tunnels outgoing packets to the gateway. The gateway removes the outer header and routes the inner packet into the public realm. It uses its binding information to send matching incoming packets back through a tunnel to the host. The RFC lists IP-IP, GRE and L2TP tunnel types.
sections.plainLanguage: The host sends a packet inside a tunnel to the gateway. The gateway uses the assigned address information to route the packet outward and return matching traffic to the host.

sections.title: Address Assignment and Flow Policy
sections.content:
RSA-IP assigns each host a unique public IP address. RSAP-IP assigns an address that may be shared and a set of ports unique for that address. Hosts and gateways must support RSAP-IP; they may also support RSA-IP.

A gateway's local flow policy controls whether it assigns an address or an address and ports. Its remote flow policy can require the host to specify a remote address, a remote address and port, or no remote destination. The host must use granted resources only as permitted by that policy.
sections.plainLanguage: RSIP can assign a public address, or an address with ports. The gateway may limit which remote address or port the host can contact with those resources.

sections.title: Registration and Leases
sections.content:
An RSIP host has one of three relationships with a gateway. An unregistered host must register before using RSIP. A registered host has a client ID and flow policy but no assigned resources. An assigned host has one or more bindings that the gateway uses to forward globally addressed packets.

Registrations and bindings have lease times in seconds. When a binding is created or extended, the registration lasts at least as long as the longest binding, so a registration does not expire while a binding remains valid.
sections.plainLanguage: A host first registers, then requests address or port resources. Each registration and binding has a lease, and the registration remains valid while any binding is still valid.

sections.title: Messages and Transport
sections.content:
Each RSIP message starts with a one-byte version, a one-byte message type and a two-byte overall length. Parameters follow: required parameters appear in a fixed order, and optional parameters may appear in any order. Parameters use a type-length-value format.

RSIP uses its own application-layer protocol over TCP or UDP. Gateways must support TCP and should support UDP. With UDP, the parties must use timeouts and retransmissions; the RFC recommends binary exponential backoff with an initial duration of 12.5 milliseconds and no more than six retries.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message identifies its version, type and length, followed by ordered parameters. If the parties use UDP, they must retry messages that do not receive a response.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Costs
sections.content:
The RFC states that RSIP does not provide security by itself. Messages are not authenticated in this specification, and hiding a private address range should not be treated as security or privacy. It recommends that a gateway prevent hosts from requesting an excessive amount of resources.

The IESG note warns of significant host and gateway changes, possible application interoperability problems and operational complexity. It says the costs and benefits should be weighed against other ways to address address shortage.
sections.plainLanguage: RSIP does not authenticate its messages, so it does not replace security protocols. The RFC also warns that hosts, gateways and network operations need changes to use it.
